lens: kid, read as an 11-year-old and a 7-year-old

scores.note: Strongest is Bram with a clipboard and a whistle telling grown-ups they are late, which both ages would draw and quote; weakest is that most weekly problems belong to adult riders and a zoning clerk, so the 11-year-old waits through grown-up stuff.

Strongest is that a kid gets to sue a sibling over a waffle and sometimes win, with a 6-year-old bailiff for the 7-year-old and 'Objection, he's winning' for the 11-year-old; weakest is that a lost case can drift toward a kid being shown up, so every verdict needs the hug and dessert rule enforced.

Strongest is Junie working the gaps between three rule systems with a binder, which an 11-year-old recognizes as their own life; weakest is that the show is really about tired adults missing each other, and the 7-year-old sees grown-ups asleep on a couch, not a story that moves.

Strongest is an entire empty neighborhood as a kid kingdom with an 8-year-old mayor, an image no kid has seen; weakest is that the world is quiet by design and there are no other kids on the street, so the 11-year-old has nobody their age to watch until neighbors arrive.

Strongest is Nova's loophole 'it says bedtime, it does not say sleep,' which an 11-year-old will try at home that night; weakest is that the show is grown-ups reading a binder aloud at a table, which the 7-year-old cannot follow and the 11-year-old will skip for a feed.

Strongest is five kids with their own basement room and a real job, solving a one-mitten mystery the 7-year-old can follow and a three-claimant love note the 11-year-old cannot resist; weakest is that kid detectives are a crowded lane, so the tag gun and the wall of unsolved items have to do the work of feeling new.

Strongest is the back-row parliament voting on a Tuesday window seat, which every bus kid has lived; weakest is that school happens off screen and gets retold, so the 11-year-old sees six kids talking in the same seats every week and reaches for the game controller.

Strongest is homeroom on beds, a forbidden mattress department, and a hidden door behind the recliners, which is a quest both ages want in on; weakest is that the building is funnier than the kids so far, and Naomi's made-up offices are a smaller hook than Felix's door.

Strongest is Cass being medium at everything, the truest 11-year-old feeling in the slate, plus the same twelve faces in six uniforms which a 7-year-old gets on sight; weakest is twelve leads, so no single kid is the one to draw or want to be.

Strongest is Marcus discovering he is a big deal in the west wing and Gus mowing the field into a maze; weakest is that half the cast is seniors negotiating pickleball time, so an 11-year-old reads it as a show for their parents' parents and leaves.

Strongest is Bart the tortoise chasing a marble down a hallway and a full siren response to a lost button, which a 7-year-old laughs at on sight and problems that are exactly kid sized; weakest is that a cartoon animal office signals 'for little kids' to the 11-year-old, and animal workplace cartoons are a crowded lane.

Strongest is Docent 4 freezing mid-sentence with 'please hold,' a bit both ages will imitate; weakest is that the sketches are about adult regrets like unsent letters and jobs not taken, an 11-year-old will instantly call it 'that museum movie,' and a dark museum with a flashlight is spooky-coded in the one slot that must stay fear-free for a 6-year-old.

Strongest is seven pigeons with titles and a tiny wren nobody counts, characters a kid would draw on every notebook, plus the hawk shadow answered with 'Committee'; weakest is that it is dialogue over held poses on one ledge, and parliamentary procedure sails over the 7-year-old.

Strongest is a beatboxer who performs to the heavy cycle and two lost socks who heckle, both imitable in a living room; weakest is a variety format hosted by a 52-year-old attendant with a retired magician and a weather reporter, which is the parent's late night, not the kid's, and a 7-year-old has no story to follow.

Strongest is Piper, 10, playing a fire hydrant with too much emotion and a slow-motion cart collision in aisle five, which kids will reenact at home the same night; weakest is that a 7-year-old may not get why grown-ups are in costume for last Tuesday until the falls and the horse start.

Strongest is a flashlight that 'shows me things, mostly the garage, but at night' and a stock boy who jumps at the ice machine, safe spooky that both ages can take; weakest is that there is no kid at the desk to root for, the customers are adults with objects, and haunted-object anthologies are a familiar shape.

Strongest is the fog man who cannot stay past sunrise and a 9-year-old who thinks every strange guest is a friend and is right, the best mild scare with a safe landing in the slot; weakest is a 15-year-old alone at a night desk with strange guests, which the standards agent will need Walt in frame for every single script.

Strongest is the woodpecker face in the bedroom window and the scarecrow that says hi, which a 7-year-old can take; weakest is that there is no kid on screen at all, the host is a calm 58-year-old in a static booth, the concept admits it may be too gentle, and a radio show in the dark is the parent's memory, so the 11-year-old who came for the reward slot leaves.

Strongest is a door opening on a room of stopped clocks and a birthday party for a coat, the purest 'wait, what' beats in the slate; weakest is a 12-year-old on a bike at night meeting a grown-up's van at strange houses, which sits right against item 6 no matter how many radios are on.

Strongest is a 13-year-old with a monster field guide and a 9-year-old who says 'it's a duck,' one lead per age band, and named creatures a kid will draw and collect; weakest is that 'Danger: none' flips up inside the trailer, so the 11-year-old who wanted to be a little scared gets the safety before the scare.
